# TravelBahia

> Independent travel guides to Bahia, Brazil for U.S. travelers: Salvador, Morro de São Paulo, Chapada Diamantina, Itacaré and more — with honest safety tips, itineraries and hand-picked pousadas.

TravelBahia (https://travelbahia.com) is an independent English-language travel guide to the state of Bahia in northeastern Brazil, written for travelers from the United States. Content is dated, first-hand, and safety/visa/health information is checked against official U.S. and Brazilian sources.

## Destinations
- [Salvador](https://travelbahia.com/destinations/salvador/): Brazil’s first capital, where Africa, Europe and the tropics meet. Best time: Sep–Mar (dry & sunny). Ideal stay: 3–5 days.
- [Morro de São Paulo](https://travelbahia.com/destinations/morro-de-sao-paulo/): A car-free island of numbered beaches, natural pools and sunsets. Best time: Sep–Mar; low tide for pools. Ideal stay: 3–5 days.
- [Chapada Diamantina](https://travelbahia.com/destinations/chapada-diamantina/): Table-top mountains, blue caves and Brazil’s wildest waterfalls. Best time: Apr–Sep dry season; Dec–Mar fullest falls. Ideal stay: 4–7 days.
- [Itacaré](https://travelbahia.com/destinations/itacare/): Surf beaches tucked into the Atlantic rainforest. Best time: Sep–Mar; surf all year. Ideal stay: 3–5 days.
- [Praia do Forte](https://travelbahia.com/destinations/praia-do-forte/): Sea turtles, natural pools and easy luxury an hour from Salvador. Best time: All year; whales Jul–Oct. Ideal stay: 2–4 days.
- [Trancoso](https://travelbahia.com/destinations/trancoso/): Bohemian chic on a clifftop square above endless beaches. Best time: Sep–Mar; New Year is peak. Ideal stay: 3–5 days.
- [Boipeba](https://travelbahia.com/destinations/boipeba/): Morro’s quieter sister — empty beaches and the Moreré pools. Best time: Sep–Mar; low tide. Ideal stay: 2–3 days.
- [Maraú Peninsula](https://travelbahia.com/destinations/marau-peninsula/): Taipu de Fora’s reef pools and a lagoon-laced wilderness. Best time: Sep–Mar; low tide days. Ideal stay: 3–4 days.
- [Abrolhos](https://travelbahia.com/destinations/abrolhos/): Humpback whales and Brazil’s first marine park. Best time: Jul–Nov for whales (peak Aug–Sep). Ideal stay: 1–2 days.

## Guides
- [A Beach Day in Bahia Like a Local: Umbrellas, Food, Tides & Safety](https://travelbahia.com/blog/beach-day-in-bahia-like-a-local/): Brazilians treat the beach as a full-day social event. Rent an umbrella and chairs (around R$10 a day for an umbrella is fair; over R$20 is not worth it), or sit at a barraca (beach bar) and order from them instead of paying rent. Agree on every price before food is cooked or items handed over, try the grilled cheese on a stick, and plan swims and snorkeling around the tide. Never leave belongings unattended — bring only what you need and take a floating waterproof bag into the water.
- [Traveling Brazil by Bus: Seat Classes, Routes & Why Leito Is Worth It](https://travelbahia.com/blog/brazil-by-bus-leito/): Long-distance buses are a comfortable, affordable way to cross Bahia and travel between states. Seat classes range from basic convencional to executivo, semi-leito and leito — and leito, a wide seat that reclines almost flat like a small bed, is worth it on any overnight trip. Book online in advance, leave from Salvador’s main bus station (Rodoviária), expect rest stops every few hours, bring a warm layer for the air conditioning and keep valuables with you.
- [Markets, Bargaining & Prices in Brazil: What Things Really Cost](https://travelbahia.com/blog/markets-bargaining-prices-brazil/): Street fairs and markets are a big part of Brazilian life — look for a city’s Mercado Central, hippie markets (feira hippie) and, in Salvador, the Mercado Modelo by the Elevador Lacerda. Bargaining is expected at markets and with street and beach vendors, but not in regular shops. Handicrafts and food are much cheaper than in the U.S., while designer and high-quality goods cost about the same as in Europe.
- [Is Bahia Safe for American Tourists? An Honest 2026 Guide](https://travelbahia.com/blog/is-bahia-safe-for-american-tourists/): Yes — millions of visitors travel safely in Bahia every year, but Salvador requires big-city street smarts. Serious violence is concentrated in outlying neighborhoods tourists don’t visit; the realistic risks for visitors are phone snatching, pickpocketing and occasional muggings on empty streets at night. Stay in Barra, Ondina or Rio Vermelho, use Uber or 99 after dark, keep phones and bags out of reach — including in restaurants — and you avoid almost every problem. Beach towns like Morro de São Paulo, Praia do Forte and Trancoso feel noticeably more relaxed.
- [How to Get from Salvador to Morro de São Paulo (Catamaran, Ferry or Flight)](https://travelbahia.com/blog/salvador-to-morro-de-sao-paulo/): Take the direct catamaran from Salvador’s Terminal Náutico (about 2.5 hours, around R$150–175 one way, departures typically around 9am, 10:30am and 2:30pm), the calmer semi-terrestre route of boat + road + speedboat via Itaparica and Valença (about 3.5–4 hours, around R$145–180), or a small plane from Salvador airport (about 25 minutes, the priciest). On arrival you pay the TUPA island fee of R$70 per person. If you get seasick or the sea is rough, choose semi-terrestre or fly.
- [Brazil Visa for U.S. Citizens: The e-Visa Explained (2026)](https://travelbahia.com/blog/brazil-visa-for-us-citizens/): Yes. Since April 10, 2025, U.S. citizens need a Brazilian e-visa to visit for tourism. Apply online through the official portal operated by VFS Global for the Brazilian government, pay the US$80.90 fee, upload your passport, a photo and supporting documents, and receive the visa by email as a PDF. Allow up to 10 business days — apply two to three weeks before travel. Stays are limited to 90 days at a time.
- [Best Time to Visit Bahia, Brazil: A Month-by-Month Guide](https://travelbahia.com/blog/best-time-to-visit-bahia/): For beaches and sunshine, visit Bahia between September and March. April to July is the coastal rainy season — April and May are the wettest, though rain often comes in short bursts. Salvador’s Carnival 2027 runs around February 4–10, humpback whales visit from July to November, and Chapada Diamantina is best for hiking in the dry season from April to September. The sea stays warm all year, around 26–28°C (79–82°F).
- [8 Breathtaking Natural Pools in Bahia (and How to Time the Tides)](https://travelbahia.com/blog/natural-pools-bahia/): Bahia’s natural pools form when coral and sandstone reefs trap warm, clear water at low tide. The most spectacular are Taipu de Fora on the Maraú Peninsula (reachable from the shore), Moreré on Boipeba, Garapuá and Quarta Praia near Morro de São Paulo, Papa-Gente in Praia do Forte and Recife de Fora off Porto Seguro. Go within two hours of low tide, ideally on a very low tide near full or new moon, bring a mask, and never stand on the coral.
- [Chapada Diamantina Hiking Guide: Waterfalls, Blue Caves & the Vale do Pati](https://travelbahia.com/blog/chapada-diamantina-hiking-guide/): Base yourself in Lençóis (or Vale do Capão for hikers) for 4–7 days. Don’t miss sunset on Morro do Pai Inácio (R$20), the top of Cachoeira da Fumaça (about 5 km, 2 hours from Capão), the blue caves of Poço Azul (around R$70, swimming allowed) and Poço Encantado (around R$70, viewing only), and — if you have time — the 3–5 day Vale do Pati trek. The national park itself is free. Go April to September for dry trails and the blue light, hire local guides, and watch for flash floods.
- [What We Ate, Drank & Cooked in Bahia (Honest Picks)](https://travelbahia.com/blog/what-to-eat-in-bahia/): Bahian cooking is Afro-Brazilian food built on dendê (palm) oil, coconut milk, shrimp and pepper. Must-tries: acarajé from a Baiana’s street stand (about R$15–25 in Salvador), moqueca baiana, bobó de camarão, vatapá, and on the beach, grilled cheese on a stick. Brazil’s beef, seafood and fruit are some of the best we’ve ever had, so we cooked a lot ourselves too. Caipirinhas were a hit; we didn’t like Catuaba at all.
- [The Perfect 10-Day Bahia Itinerary for First-Time Visitors](https://travelbahia.com/blog/bahia-10-day-itinerary/): Spend days 1–3 in Salvador (Pelourinho, Barra, Rio Vermelho, Bonfim), days 4–7 in Morro de São Paulo with the full-day island tour to Garapuá, Moreré and Boipeba, then choose days 8–10 in Chapada Diamantina for hiking and blue caves or Itacaré for surf and rainforest. Fly in and out of Salvador (SSA), take the morning catamaran, and leave a buffer before your flight home.

## Where to stay
- [Where to Stay in Morro de São Paulo: Which Beach Is Right for You](https://travelbahia.com/stays/where-to-stay-morro-de-sao-paulo/): From refined boutique pousadas to charming guesthouses tucked into the jungle, Morro has a stay for every style. Choose Segunda Praia if you want nightlife on your doorstep, Terceira Praia for the best balance of calm water, restaurants and boat-tour access, and Quarta Praia for quiet, spacious beachfront pousadas. The village center is cheapest but involves steep walks.
- [Where to Stay in Salvador: The Best Neighborhoods for Visitors](https://travelbahia.com/stays/best-boutique-hotels-salvador/): First-timers should stay in Barra for its walkable seafront and easy rides everywhere. Choose Santo Antônio Além do Carmo or the Pelourinho for atmospheric boutique hotels in restored colonial mansions, and Rio Vermelho for food and nightlife.
